name_zh: 富布瑟林茶园大吉岭红茶
cultivar: Phoobsering 312 (P312) is named after this estate; the bushes behind a given lot vary.
processing: Orthodox Darjeeling making, with the garden also known for oolong-style tea. Oxidation depends on the lot and season.
harvest_season: Darjeeling flushes generally run from spring into autumn; plucking there is by hand every five to ten days.
appearance_dry: Typically twisted olive-brown leaf with some pale tips, varying with flush and style.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold in lighter lots, moving to amber in summer tea.
appearance_wet: Mixed green and copper whole-leaf pieces, as is usual for orthodox Darjeeling.
taste_profile: This garden's own cup is little described beyond praise for its oolong. Typical of Darjeeling, expect florals in spring lots and riper fruit in summer ones.

brewing.notes: Western-style suits most lots. Try oolong-style lots with more leaf and shorter steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, usually with the garden name on the label, and organic lots are offered. Current-season tea is the norm, and spring lots are best drunk young.
description:
Phoobsering is one of the older plantations in Darjeeling's West valley, covering 510 hectares. Its name also turns up in a less obvious place: the cultivar Phoobsering 312, one of the plantings adapted specifically for Darjeeling.

The garden works in the usual Darjeeling way, with distinct seasonal flushes, and its oolong has a particular following. Black and oolong-style lots from the same place can be quite different teas, so read the label.

Detailed tasting notes for the garden are scarce. As with other Darjeelings, a spring lot is light and floral, a summer one fuller and fruitier. Use a little less heat for the delicate lots.

Look for the flush, year and style when buying. The name also appears as Phoobshering, so both spellings are worth searching.
history: The estate is dated to 1856-1860, when the Darjeeling Tea Company set it up along with Ging, Takdah and Ambootia. It takes its name from Phurpu Tshering, a Sikkimese man and brother of Chebu Lama, the name Phurpu marking his birth on a Thursday. Accounts differ on his Lepcha or Bhutia descent.
